Module 6: Pseudotime Trajectory Analysis

Single Cell Workshop

2026-04-23

1 Introduction

In Module 5 we annotated each query cell with a continuous score on every reference phenotype. Those scores already hint at a foetal→adult gradient within cardiomyocytes — recall the age-group scores climbing smoothly from fetal to old. Module 6 turns that hint into a single scalar per cell: pseudotime.

Pseudotime is a real number per cell such that cells that are close in the underlying biological process have close values. It is not real time, and the absolute scale is not identified — it is an ordering. Direction (which end is “early”) is a separate question, and for principal-curve methods like slingshot it has to be supplied externally. This is exactly where the Φ-Space age-group scores earn their keep: the cluster with the highest mean fetal score is an obvious anchor for the start of the cardiomyocyte maturation trajectory.

1.1 Two methods, two embeddings

We run two families of method, chosen to be maximally complementary:

  • Slingshot — a principal-curve method. Cluster cells, build a minimum spanning tree on the cluster centroids, fit a smooth curve through each lineage, project every cell onto the curve. Pseudotime = arc length. We run slingshot twice: once on PCA of scran logcounts (the classical choice), once on the Φ-Space score matrix. Same cells, same clusters, same anchor. Any difference between the two pseudotimes is an embedding effect.
  • DPT (diffusion pseudotime) via destiny — a diffusion / random walk method. Build a Gaussian-kernel affinity graph, eigendecompose the associated Markov chain, and use accumulated transition probability from a root as pseudotime. We run DPT once, on PCA of scran logcounts, as a cross-check: a different statistical machinery on the same embedding as the first slingshot run.

One thing destiny gets “for free” that slingshot does not: endpoint detection. Without a tips argument, destiny picks trajectory tips automatically from the diffusion-map geometry. We still choose to pin the root at the highest-fetal-score cell, for comparability, but the auto-detection is a genuine advantage of diffusion methods for exploratory work where you do not yet know which end is which. The flip side — less explicit control over endpoints — is a feature, not a defect; it is just a different point on the “automated vs controllable” axis.

1.2 Learning objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • Explain what pseudotime is, what it is not, and why it needs an external directionality anchor for principal-curve methods.
  • Fit a slingshot trajectory on two different embeddings and interpret the difference.
  • Fit a DPT trajectory via destiny and compare it against slingshot.
  • Use a simple multi-pseudotime correlation matrix as a sanity check on any single trajectory result.
  • Save a pseudotime-annotated CM subset for Module 7.

2 Load Libraries and Module 5 Output

library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(slingshot)
library(destiny)
library(scater)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(patchwork)
library(RColorBrewer)

The handoff from Module 5 is a single file — the query SCE with PhiSpace scores in reducedDim, scran logcounts in assay(query, "logcounts"), and per-cell annotations (PhiCellType, PhiCellTypeBroad, PhiAge, group, etc.) in colData.

query <- readRDS("../results/05_phispace_query.rds")

cat("Assays:      ", paste(assayNames(query), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Assays:       counts, logcounts
cat("reducedDims: ", paste(reducedDimNames(query), collapse = ", "), "\n")
## reducedDims:  PhiSpace
cat("Cells:       ", ncol(query), "\n")
## Cells:        10000
cat("Broad types: ", paste(sort(unique(query$PhiCellTypeBroad)),
                            collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Broad types:  Adipocyte, Cardiomyocyte, Endocardial, Endothelial, Epicardial, Fibroblast, LEC, Lymphoid, Mast, Myeloid, Neuronal, Pericyte, vSMC
results_dir <- "../results"
dir.create(results_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

3 Subset to Cardiomyocytes

Cardiomyocytes carry the foetal→adult maturation signal we want to trace. Fibroblasts and the other lineages are interesting but secondary; running pseudotime on the whole query would mix several biological processes into one trajectory.

cm <- query[, query$PhiCellTypeBroad == "Cardiomyocyte"]
cat("Cardiomyocytes:", ncol(cm), "\n")
## Cardiomyocytes: 5411
print(table(cm$group))
## 
## adult fetal young 
##   409  4016   986
print(sort(table(cm$PhiCellType), decreasing = TRUE))
## 
##  Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_metabolic                     Cardiomyocyte:Other 
##                                    1557                                    1375 
##                 Cardiomyocyte:Metabolic Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_conduction 
##                                    1116                                     652 
##          Cardiomyocyte:DCM_HCM_enriched              Cardiomyocyte:Inflammatory 
##                                     439                                     211 
##                  Cardiomyocyte:Stressed 
##                                      61

The fine Φ-Space labels give us biologically meaningful CM clusters (Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_*, :Metabolic, :Stressed, …) without any extra Leiden pass. We’ll reuse them as the clustering input to slingshot below.

4 Expression-Based Embedding: PCA on scran logcounts

For the “classical” slingshot run we need an embedding of gene expression. We compute a standard HVG → PCA pipeline on the scran logcounts we already have from Module 5.

pca_cache <- file.path(results_dir, "06_cm_pca.rds")

if (file.exists(pca_cache)) {
    cm <- readRDS(pca_cache)
    message("Loaded cached CM object with PCA from ", pca_cache)
} else {
    # Highly variable gene selection
    gene_var <- rowVars(as.matrix(logcounts(cm)))
    names(gene_var) <- rownames(cm)
    n_hvg <- min(2000, nrow(cm))
    hvg <- names(sort(gene_var, decreasing = TRUE))[seq_len(n_hvg)]

    pca <- prcomp(t(as.matrix(logcounts(cm)[hvg, ])),
                  center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
    reducedDim(cm, "PCA") <- pca$x[, 1:20]
    saveRDS(cm, pca_cache)
}

cat("PCA dims:      ", paste(dim(reducedDim(cm, "PCA")), collapse = " x "), "\n")
## PCA dims:       5411 x 20
cat("PhiSpace dims: ", paste(dim(reducedDim(cm, "PhiSpace")),
                             collapse = " x "), "\n")
## PhiSpace dims:  5411 x 28

We keep 20 PCs. That is a defensible default for single-cell data of this size; tunePhiSpace-style cross-validation of the component count is possible but not the point here.

5 Picking the Trajectory Anchor

For slingshot we need a start.clus. Rather than hand-picking a root cell, we pick the CM cluster whose mean score on the reference fetal phenotype is highest — a fully data-driven anchor.

phi_scores <- reducedDim(cm, "PhiSpace")
fetal_score <- phi_scores[, "fetal"]

anchor_tbl <- tibble(
    cluster = cm$PhiCellType,
    fetal   = fetal_score
) |>
    group_by(cluster) |>
    summarise(mean_fetal = mean(fetal), n = n(),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_fetal))

print(anchor_tbl)
## # A tibble: 7 × 3
##   cluster                                 mean_fetal     n
##   <chr>                                        <dbl> <int>
## 1 Cardiomyocyte:Other                          0.667  1375
## 2 Cardiomyocyte:Metabolic                      0.665  1116
## 3 Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_metabolic       0.578  1557
## 4 Cardiomyocyte:Stressed                       0.554    61
## 5 Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_conduction     -0.326   652
## 6 Cardiomyocyte:Inflammatory                  -0.404   211
## 7 Cardiomyocyte:DCM_HCM_enriched              -0.432   439
start_cluster <- anchor_tbl$cluster[1]
cat("\nAnchor (start.clus):", start_cluster, "\n")
## 
## Anchor (start.clus): Cardiomyocyte:Other

We also pre-compute the per-cell root index for destiny, which wants a cell rather than a cluster.

start_cells <- which(cm$PhiCellType == start_cluster)
root_cell   <- start_cells[which.max(fetal_score[start_cells])]
cat("Root cell index:", root_cell, "\n")
## Root cell index: 1800

6 Slingshot on Φ-Space Scores

sling_phi_cache <- file.path(results_dir, "06_slingshot_phispace.rds")

if (file.exists(sling_phi_cache)) {
    sling_phi <- readRDS(sling_phi_cache)
    message("Loaded cached slingshot-PhiSpace result")
} else {
    sling_phi <- slingshot(
        reducedDim(cm, "PhiSpace"),
        clusterLabels = cm$PhiCellType,
        start.clus    = start_cluster,
        dist.method   = "simple"
    )
    saveRDS(sling_phi, sling_phi_cache)
}

cat("Lineages found:\n")
## Lineages found:
print(slingLineages(sling_phi))
## $Lineage1
## [1] "Cardiomyocyte:Other"                    
## [2] "Cardiomyocyte:Metabolic"                
## [3] "Cardiomyocyte:Stressed"                 
## [4] "Cardiomyocyte:Inflammatory"             
## [5] "Cardiomyocyte:DCM_HCM_enriched"         
## [6] "Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_conduction"
## 
## $Lineage2
## [1] "Cardiomyocyte:Other"                   
## [2] "Cardiomyocyte:Metabolic"               
## [3] "Cardiomyocyte:Fetal_enriched_metabolic"

Slingshot’s slingPseudotime() returns one column per lineage; for a predominantly linear CM maturation trajectory we expect one dominant lineage.

pt_phi <- slingPseudotime(sling_phi)
cm$pt_sling_phi <- rowMeans(pt_phi, na.rm = TRUE)
summary(cm$pt_sling_phi)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
## 0.02968 1.49515 1.82848 2.23352 3.01053 5.27565

7 Slingshot on PCA of Expression

Same clusters, same anchor, different embedding.

sling_pca_cache <- file.path(results_dir, "06_slingshot_pca.rds")

if (file.exists(sling_pca_cache)) {
    sling_pca <- readRDS(sling_pca_cache)
    message("Loaded cached slingshot-PCA result")
} else {
    sling_pca <- slingshot(
        reducedDim(cm, "PCA"),
        clusterLabels = cm$PhiCellType,
        start.clus    = start_cluster,
        dist.method   = "simple"
    )
    saveRDS(sling_pca, sling_pca_cache)
}

pt_pca <- slingPseudotime(sling_pca)
cm$pt_sling_pca <- rowMeans(pt_pca, na.rm = TRUE)
summary(cm$pt_sling_pca)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    0.00   27.61   33.56   42.92   63.79  127.60

8 DPT via destiny on PCA

For the diffusion cross-check we build a diffusion map on the PCA embedding and compute DPT from the same root cell we used above.

dpt_cache <- file.path(results_dir, "06_dpt_pca.rds")

if (file.exists(dpt_cache)) {
    dpt <- readRDS(dpt_cache)
    message("Loaded cached DPT result")
} else {
    dm  <- DiffusionMap(as.matrix(reducedDim(cm, "PCA")),
                        n_eigs = 20, sigma = "local", verbose = FALSE)
    dpt <- DPT(dm, tips = root_cell)
    saveRDS(dpt, dpt_cache)
}

cm$pt_dpt_pca <- dpt$dpt
summary(cm$pt_dpt_pca)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##  0.0000  0.4120  0.6941  5.4210 16.1667 20.6281

A note on what we did not pass: if we had called DPT(dm) with no tips, destiny would have auto-detected trajectory endpoints from the diffusion-map geometry — that is the “endpoints for free” property of diffusion methods. We pass the root explicitly here only to keep destiny’s pseudotime directly comparable with the two slingshot runs.

9 Three-Way Comparison

All three pseudotimes live on different absolute scales, so we rescale each to [0, 1] before comparing.

rescale01 <- function(x) {
    x <- x - min(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    x / max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}

cm$pt_sling_phi_01 <- rescale01(cm$pt_sling_phi)
cm$pt_sling_pca_01 <- rescale01(cm$pt_sling_pca)
cm$pt_dpt_pca_01   <- rescale01(cm$pt_dpt_pca)

pt_mat <- as.data.frame(colData(cm)[,
    c("pt_sling_phi_01", "pt_sling_pca_01", "pt_dpt_pca_01")])
colnames(pt_mat) <- c("slingshot/PhiSpace",
                      "slingshot/PCA",
                      "DPT/PCA")

9.1 Correlation matrix

round(cor(pt_mat, use = "complete.obs", method = "spearman"), 3)
##                    slingshot/PhiSpace slingshot/PCA DPT/PCA
## slingshot/PhiSpace              1.000         0.782   0.602
## slingshot/PCA                   0.782         1.000   0.742
## DPT/PCA                         0.602         0.742   1.000

Spearman (rank) correlation is the right scalar summary because each method has a different absolute scale and we only care about the order of cells.

9.2 Pairs plot

pt_long <- pt_mat |>
    rownames_to_column("cell") |>
    mutate(group = cm$group[match(cell, colnames(cm))])

make_pair <- function(x, y) {
    ggplot(pt_long, aes(.data[[x]], .data[[y]], colour = group)) +
        geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
        geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0,
                    linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
        scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
        theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
        theme(legend.position = "none") +
        labs(x = x, y = y)
}

pairs <- list(
    make_pair("slingshot/PhiSpace", "slingshot/PCA"),
    make_pair("slingshot/PhiSpace", "DPT/PCA"),
    make_pair("slingshot/PCA",      "DPT/PCA")
)

wrap_plots(pairs, ncol = 2) +
    plot_annotation(title = "Pairwise agreement between pseudotimes")

Read the three panels as answers to three different questions:

  • slingshot/PhiSpace vs slingshot/PCA — pure embedding effect. Same method, same clusters, same anchor. Disagreement here says the choice of embedding moves the trajectory.
  • slingshot vs DPT on PCA — pure method effect. Same embedding, different trajectory family. Disagreement says the result is geometry-specific.
  • slingshot/PhiSpace vs DPT/PCA — the hardest diagonal; if this one agrees, the trajectory is probably robust.

9.3 Pseudotime vs donor stage

box_df <- pt_long |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(
        cols = c("slingshot/PhiSpace", "slingshot/PCA", "DPT/PCA"),
        names_to = "method", values_to = "pseudotime"
    ) |>
    mutate(method = factor(method,
        levels = c("slingshot/PhiSpace", "slingshot/PCA", "DPT/PCA")))

ggplot(box_df, aes(group, pseudotime, fill = group)) +
    geom_violin(scale = "width", alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, outlier.size = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    facet_wrap(~ method, nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Donor stage", y = "Pseudotime (rescaled)",
         fill = "Stage",
         title = "Do pseudotimes recover the known foetal → adult ordering?") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

The donor stage (group) is held-out information: none of the three pseudotime methods saw it. If the violins step upward cleanly from fetal to adult on all three panels, the trajectory is recovering the real maturation order.

10 Handing Off to Module 7

We save the CM object with all three pseudotimes attached so Module 7 can use them as the time axis for gene-regulatory-network inference.

final_cache <- file.path(results_dir, "06_cm_pseudotime.rds")
saveRDS(cm, final_cache)
cat("Annotated CM object at", final_cache, "\n")
## Annotated CM object at ../results/06_cm_pseudotime.rds

The object carries, in addition to everything Module 5 handed us:

  • reducedDim(cm, "PCA") — 20 PCs on scran logcounts of HVGs.
  • colData(cm)$pt_sling_phi / pt_sling_pca / pt_dpt_pca — raw pseudotimes from the three runs.
  • colData(cm)$pt_*_01 — the same pseudotimes rescaled to [0, 1] for cross-method comparison.

For Module 7 we will primarily use pt_sling_phi — the Φ-Space slingshot pseudotime — as the canonical time axis. The other two live in the object for optional sensitivity analyses.

11 Summary

  • Pseudotime gives a scalar ordering of cells along a biological process; it is not real time, and its direction for principal-curve methods comes from an external anchor.
  • Slingshot is our primary method: cluster centroids → MST → principal curves → arc-length pseudotime. We ran it on both a PCA-of-expression embedding and on the Φ-Space score matrix to isolate the effect of the embedding.
  • DPT via destiny is our diffusion cross-check on the PCA embedding. It adds two useful things: (i) automatic endpoint detection, and
    1. a fundamentally different statistical object (random-walk probabilities rather than arc length), which catches principal-curve artefacts.
  • The three-pseudotime comparison is not bureaucratic — it tells you whether your trajectory is robust to embedding choice, method choice, or both.
